analysis.one_liner: Steeply raises tobacco taxes and puts the money into a trust fund for children's health coverage and anti-smoking programs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, and other tobacco products in stages, reaching about 94.5 cents per pack of cigarettes by 2002 on top of an increase already enacted in 1997. All of the new revenue would have gone into a dedicated trust fund: 75% to states for tobacco education, quitting programs, children's health insurance, and nutrition programs for women and children; 25% to federal programs including tobacco control, medical research, and aid to tobacco-farming communities. It also would have removed federal limits on health warnings in tobacco advertising.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families gain new funding for the Children's Health Insurance Program, WIC nutrition aid, and maternal health services. Smokers who quit or never start benefit from funded prevention and cessation programs, and higher prices are the most effective lever for reducing smoking. States get dedicated money for anti-tobacco education and counter-advertising, and tobacco-farming communities get federal compensation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, low-income families, and state health programs

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal cigarette excise tax in stages from $12 to $94.50 per thousand (about 94.5 cents per pack) by 2002, on top of the increase in the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, with all other tobacco products raised proportionally.

Deposits all new revenue into a PHAER Trust Fund, with 75% distributed to states for tobacco education, prevention, cessation and treatment, the Children's Health Insurance Program, WIC or maternal and child health block grants, cancer prevention programs, and general health care block grants.

Sends 25% to federal programs, including FDA tobacco control, protection of tobacco farmers and their communities, NIH disease research, CDC smoking-reduction efforts, and a national counter-advertising campaign.
Repeals federal provisions that restrict health-related statements on cigarette and smokeless tobacco products and their advertisements.

States the sense of the Senate that any final comprehensive tobacco bill funded by the trust fund must include penalties for advertising that targets children, full FDA authority to regulate tobacco as a drug, elimination of secondhand smoke in public and private buildings, ingredient disclosure, and a ban on using federal resources to promote tobacco sales abroad.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers pay through higher prices — federal taxes are passed on in the retail price of cigarettes and other tobacco products. Tobacco manufacturers, wholesalers (who owe new floor-stocks taxes on inventory when rates rise), and retailers bear reduced sales and compliance costs. Tobacco farmers lose demand but receive a dedicated federal program to protect their financial well-being.

drawbacks.text: Tobacco excise taxes are regressive: lower-income smokers who continue smoking pay the most, since the tax is the same per pack regardless of income. The bill raises the cigarette tax roughly eightfold by 2002.

The tax falls on a legal product sold to adult consumers, and the bill's own design acknowledges the disruption by dedicating a quarter of the federal share to shielding tobacco-farming families and communities from the loss of income.

Higher prices can push some sales toward smuggled or previously exported product relanded in the U.S.; the bill responds with new penalties and import restrictions rather than eliminating the incentive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside was large: price increases are the best-documented way to cut smoking, especially among teenagers, and the bill recycled every dollar into children's health insurance, nutrition aid, and quitting programs rather than general revenue. The honest cost is regressivity — the heaviest burden lands on lower-income adults who keep smoking — though the bill partially offsets this by funding the health programs those same families rely on. On balance it was a well-targeted public health measure whose main weakness was the political difficulty of its main feature.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee took no action after the bill was referred to it, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on October 29, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
Two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican senator did.
The committee never reported the bill, and no committee or floor vote was ever held; the only further action in the record is a second set of introductory remarks by the sponsor in February 1998.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and bills not passed by both chambers within a Congress die and must be reintroduced from scratch.
This bill arrived in the middle of the 1997-98 national debate over comprehensive tobacco legislation, which produced no enacted law in that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and sellers, who avoided a cigarette tax that would have risen to nearly a dollar a pack, kept prices and sales unchanged. The children who would have been covered through the new CHIP and WIC funding received nothing, and no comprehensive tobacco law passed in that Congress.

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks on the floor twice, and served as its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never reported it out, held no markup, and never sent it to the floor.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate calendar in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split appears in the record; all three senators attached to the bill were Democrats and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill multiplies the federal cigarette excise tax roughly eightfold by 2002 and raises taxes on cigars, smokeless tobacco, and pipe tobacco proportionally, directly cutting into sales. The industry's financial interest ran against the bill's public health purpose, and the bill also would have stripped federal limits on health warnings in advertising.

Their product would be taxed at sharply higher rates, shrinking demand, but the bill dedicates a quarter of the federal share of the trust fund to protecting the financial well-being of tobacco farmers, their families, and their communities.

The bill imposes floor-stocks taxes on existing inventory on each tax increase date, tightens rules on imported and exported products with new forfeiture and penalty provisions, and subjects retailers to higher prices that depress sales.

industries.industry: State public health programs and children's health coverage
industries.note: CHIP, WIC, maternal and child health block grants, and state anti-smoking programs would have received guaranteed, dedicated funding streams on top of existing appropriations, with states required to show the money supplements rather than replaces their own spending.
